meta: A garden grotto of the Medici in Stefano della Bella's etching The Grotto of Pan and Fame, from a series on the Medici gardens.
about: This etching is one of a series Stefano della Bella made of the Medici gardens. He was born in Florence and worked a great deal for the Medici there. He also spent time in Rome and Paris between 1638 and 1650. The museum calls him a prolific graphic artist who made over 1,000 etchings, most of them from his imagination.

meta: Jan Harmensz Muller's engraving of Adriaen de Vries's Rape of a Sabine, seen from the side, from a series of three views, about 1598.
about: Jan Harmensz Muller engraved Adriaen de Vries's sculpture Rape of a Sabine from three different positions, and this is the side view. The sculpture was made in the 16th century too, but it copies the look of antique bronzes. The museum says the series shows off Muller's skill with the burin and his ability to make a print look like sculpture in the round. The story suits the job. Roman soldiers seizing brides give plenty of twisting, clashing bodies to draw.

meta: Jove hurls thunderbolts at giants storming heaven in Johann Michael Rottmayr's ceiling-style painting from about 1695.
about: Jove rears back his fist, ready to send the giants who have climbed up to attack heaven tumbling back to earth. Gleaming thunderbolts loom overhead. Jove is the Roman god also called Jupiter. The museum reads the bold brushwork, vivid colors and forward-tilted compositions as signs that this painting and its companions hung over doorways, giving viewers below a forceful illusion. Sharp contrasts of light and dark, called chiaroscuro, push the intensity higher.

meta: Studies of a male nude on tan paper for Hercules in François Lemoyne's Hercules and Omphale, painted in Rome in 1724.
about: Several studies of a male nude are spread across a tan sheet. François Lemoyne drew them to prepare the figure of Hercules in his painting Hercules and Omphale, finished in Rome in 1724. In the myth, Omphale forces the reluctant hero to spin wool like a woman. The drawing weaves together red, black and white chalks, a mix Antoine Watteau had made famous a decade earlier. The museum sees the grace of French Rococo in it, along with the force of Michelangelo's Sistine Ignudi.

meta: A single boat on a still lake at the North Woods Club in the Adirondacks: Winslow Homer's 1892 watercolor The Lone Boat.
about: Trees on the shore and their reflections form a nearly symmetrical design along a strong horizon. The museum compares it to a wet sheet folded at the center and blotted. Winslow Homer made the sky with several colors and many techniques: resist, blotting, scraping and wet-into-wet brushwork. The museum says the result gives a strong sense of movement, with clouds gathering and breaking up while the light shifts. It also reads the picture as a fisherman's communion with nature, helped by the way watercolor lets man and landscape run together.

meta: A forest framing a river and mountains beyond: Julie Hart Beers's landscape Looking upon the River, painted around 1880.
about: In the foreground a forest crowds in thickly. Beyond it, a waterway and mountains glow with light. Julie Hart Beers used quick brushwork, with a few flourishes to suggest two or three figures beside a boat at the center. She built a successful landscape career from the 1860s on, helped by her brothers, who were painters too and gave her training and studio space. She knew other women artists in New York City. Beers also earned money by teaching and by leading sketching trips for women through New England and the Adirondacks.

meta: A shopkeeper with a flower and a bell in Gustave Courbet's Mère Grégoire, painted from 1855 and reworked until 1859.
about: The woman at the counter comes from a popular song by Pierre-Jean de Béranger, whose Madame Grégoire ran a brothel. Courbet began the picture in 1855 as a simple head on a horizontal canvas. Between 1857 and 1859 he enlarged it into a full scene. Coins lie scattered on the marble counter, a ledger sits under her right hand, and the bell for calling her employees sits under the other. The museum thinks the flower, in the blue, white and red of the French flag, may be a protest against censorship and against the Second Empire itself.

meta: Joseph Wright of Derby in a fur cap and black hat, lit by a single source: his self-portrait from the 1760s.
about: Joseph Wright painted himself at night, wearing an unusual black hat, in a mood of pensive challenge to both himself and the viewer. He lived mostly in Derby, where he ran a successful portrait practice. He was always interested in what a single light source, such as a candle, does to shadows. The museum says the strong chiaroscuro of Thomas Frye's mezzotints influenced him. In the mid-1760s Wright made several dramatically lit self-portraits in oil, charcoal and pastel.

meta: An illuminated M for St. Andrew's feast, cut from a Ferrara Cathedral choir book, by Jacopo Filippo d'Argenta, about 1480.
about: The big letter M opens the chant for the mass on the feast of Saint Andrew, November 30. That date is also the start of Advent. The leaf was cut from a volume in a large set of choir books ordered for Ferrara Cathedral by Bartolomeo delle Rovere, Bishop of Ferrara and a nephew of Pope Sixtus IV. His arms are in the round panel at the bottom, an oak tree under a patriarchal cross. Payment records show that Argenta worked on the books from 1478 to 1486.

meta: Odilon Redon's 1897 color lithograph Beatrice, the woman who inspired Dante, his fullest experiment with color printing.
about: Beatrice appears often in Odilon Redon's work, and this is the woman who inspired the poet Dante. He had made a pastel of her about ten years earlier. The museum calls the print his fullest experiment with color lithography, and the only work in which he used a full range of tones. Redon made it with his regular collaborators of the 1890s, the printer Auguste Clot and the publisher Ambroise Vollard. Muted shades give her a ghostly presence.

meta: A round Virgin and Child with the young John the Baptist from the workshop of Sandro Botticelli, about 1490.
about: The round format, called a tondo, became popular in Florence in the 1440s. It was made for homes, not churches. The shape is hard to compose in, and the artist had to keep it balanced. The museum says the attribution has been debated. Botticelli often worked with students, among them Filippino Lippi. Few specialists doubt that Botticelli himself painted the central passages: the faces, the graceful poses and the thin veil. Someone else in his studio probably did Mary's blue garment, which is also the most heavily restored part.

meta: Lions and tigers play among peonies and bamboo on gold foil in Yamaguchi Sekkei's painting of 1668.
about: Lions and tigers romp among peonies and bamboo against a background of gold foil. The gold did a job as well as decorating. Traditional Japanese rooms had no windows, so light came from portable oil lamps and wax candles, and reflective surfaces made it go further. The painter, Yamaguchi Sekkei, lived and studied in Kyoto at the Kano school studio, the center of traditional painting in Japan since 1500.

meta: A woman looks at the evening sky among bare trees, thistles and a spider web in Caspar David Friedrich's woodcut of 1803.
about: For Friedrich, landscape expressed spirituality and a personal link to God. He isolated the tree, the spider web and the thistles and drew each in sharp detail. The museum says this makes familiar things feel unsettled and hints at a hidden, sacred meaning. The woman gazes at the evening sky, and the museum sees her as sharing our puzzle over what the scene means. Bare trees, thistles, a caught fly and the setting sun all point to mortality. Friedrich used a theme here that he would return to often.

meta: The Chinese Room at Middleton Park, Oxfordshire, with painted wall paper and bamboo furniture, watercolor by William Alfred Delamotte.
about: Painted Chinese paper covers the walls of this room, bordered in blue and decorated with Chinese characters. Bamboo furniture stands about. The museum points to a Chinese pane in the transom above the doorway to the conservatory, and to a japanned door. It says all of this shows how popular chinoiserie was in the Regency period. William Alfred Delamotte recorded the room at Middleton Park in Oxfordshire, looking toward the conservatory.

meta: Mrs. William B. Cabot, wife of a Boston engineer and friend of Abbott Handerson Thayer, painted partly in England.
about: Abbott Thayer carried this canvas to Cornwall, England, and took Mrs. Cabot's dress along so he could look at it while he finished the painting. She was the wife of William Brooks Cabot, a Boston civil engineer and a close friend of the artist. Thayer showed the finished portrait at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston in 1900. Two years later he showed it in Philadelphia with changes. He told his wife the new hands and right arm he added at the end made Mrs. C.

meta: A long-haired man in a lace collar painted by Cornelius Johnson around 1640, once thought to be Henry, Prince of Wales.
about: When this portrait arrived at the Smithsonian, people took the sitter for Henry, Prince of Wales, who died in 1612. Curators doubted that after comparing his face with portraits of the prince made in life. His long hair, lace collar and showy sleeves mark him as a cavalier, a supporter of the king in the civil war that later drove Cornelius Johnson to Holland. Johnson was still in England when he painted it, and held the title of his Majesty's servant as picture drawer. The attorney Ralph Cross Johnson left the painting to the national collection.

meta: A family beside a lake in the glow of the setting sun: Robert S. Duncanson's Ohio River valley landscape from the 1850s.
about: Robert S. Duncanson painted romantic views of the Ohio River valley near his home in Cincinnati in the late 1850s. This one shows a family enjoying a peaceful spot by a lake. The museum says such pictures suggest the nineteenth-century belief that God made the wilderness for people to enjoy. The setting sun lights up the tree in the foreground with glowing colors, and the museum reads that as a divine light watching over the countryside.

meta: A portrait of Ru-ton-ye-wee-ma, wife of White Cloud, one of the Iowa visitors who joined George Catlin in London in the 1840s.
about: Strutting Pigeon was one of fourteen Iowa who joined George Catlin in London in the 1840s, when he went to Europe to show and promote his Indian Gallery. Catlin eventually put the visitors in his show, where they danced and sang. People objected from the start, charging him with exploiting them. He replied that he was rescuing Indians brought over by unscrupulous promoters. Then he kept adding new acts, such as riding and tipi-building at Vauxhall Gardens, and that hurt his credibility. These portraits of Iowa women were probably painted in London in 1844.

meta: A nude Venus reclines in a landscape, engraved in dots by Giulio Campagnola around 1508.
about: Giulio Campagnola introduced the dot manner, and this reclining Venus shows it. Dots and flicks made with the point of the burin build the shading. That allowed a much wider range of tone and softer shifts from dark to light. The museum says the effect imitates sfumato, the soft atmosphere that Venetian painters such as Giorgione were after, and it sees Giorgione's influence here and perhaps even his collaboration. This is a rare early impression. A female nude in a landscape would soon become a Venetian specialty.

meta: Quick brushstrokes catch a spring breeze over the water in Childe Hassam's Spring, Navesink Highlands, New Jersey.
about: Leaves flicker and the water ripples in this view of New Jersey's Navesink Highlands. Childe Hassam lived in New York. He often left the city to paint landscapes and small villages in New England. Here he used quick brushstrokes to show a cool spring breeze. Once he had picked a frame, he wrote to his patron William T. Evans that he was glad to say it looked as fine as anything anywhere in the world.

meta: George Inness's Niagara Falls from the 1880s, painted without the bridges, hotels and signs that crowded the site.
about: Niagara Falls is one of the most painted and photographed places in the United States. George Inness made seven oil paintings of it in the 1880s and 1890s, more than of any other place at the time. By 1895 the area was crowded with hotels and souvenir shops. Inness wanted to bring back the natural terror and awe of the falls. So he left out every bridge, hotel and sign.

meta: President Andrew Johnson tramples Radical Republicans on a horse called Constitution in The Veto Galop, a music cover from 1866.
about: Andrew Johnson rides a horse labeled Constitution, raises a veto in one hand, and tramples Frederick Douglass, a stack of bureau drawers and several Radical Republican congressmen. This lithograph covers the sheet music for The Veto Galop. It was inspired by his veto of the Freedmen's Bureau Act, a law meant to help freed slaves and poor white Southerners with food, housing, education, health care and jobs. Johnson thought it gave the federal government too much power. A shop sign hints at his refusal to waste ammunition on dead ducks, a dig at the editor John Forney. Congress overturned the veto in July 1866.

meta: Smoking sheds and slag heaps with no workers in sight: Carl Redin's 1933 view of the Madrid coal mine in New Mexico.
about: Rusty, hulking buildings lead to the coal mines of Madrid in New Mexico, and no person is in sight. Smoke fouls the air. Slag heaps and machines cover the hills. Carl Redin usually painted pretty New Mexico scenery. To find the American Scene that the PWAP asked for, he turned to the mines. Madrid was a company town where the company owned the mines, stores and houses. It laid on distractions like a baseball team and Christmas lights so famous that tourists came. Redin chose the grim part instead. Except for the train engineer, all the men are underground.

meta: An abstracted landscape of trees by Will Henry Stevens, shaped by Song Dynasty painting he first saw at the Freer around 1912.
about: Trees dissolve into an abstracted landscape in this untitled work by Will Henry Stevens. Much of his art shows respect for the natural world. Though he grew up in the Midwest, he often painted the wilderness of North Carolina, Tennessee, Georgia and Virginia, and the museum says Song Dynasty painting influenced him. He first saw it at the Freer Gallery in Washington around 1912.
